Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics. [open SIL PDF, the Internet Archive snapshot 2024-11-04 ofhttps://www.sil.org/system/files/reapdata/23/85/34/23853451869958568538398841625100014874/Nii_Phonology.pdf]
catalog_locator: §8 'The Phonological Word', pp. 70-71. Supporting: §7 p.69, §2 p.40, §4.2 p.55, §9 p.72, §10.1 p.73.
catalog_quote: The phonological word in Nii consists of one to five syllables with one primary stress ˊ (a composite of higher pitch and intensity) which is unpredicable except in the following cases. In verbs, stress falls on the final syllable of words with two or more syllables. When the verb includes a negative affix a secondary stress ¯ occurs. When the final syllable is a future suffix the primary stress falls on it and the secondary stress falls on the negative affix; in all other cases the primary stress falls on the negative affix and the secondary stress falls on the final syllable. [examples p.71: /nonáɬmīn/ 'we didn't eat', /punɛ̄nmbí/ 'I will not go', /ninɛ́ndzɩpīn/ 'we didn't talk', /pináɬīm/ 'he doesn't know'; TWO-SYLLABLES: /řómbu/ 'sweet potato', /ndambí/ 'green's', /ɛ́ndɩ/ 'one', /ɛndɛ́/ 'the same', /múini/ 'lizzard', /tɩřá/ 'banana', /kíɬɩp/ 'duck']

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: VERBATIM CHECK of the compiler quotes (viewed as page scan of scan pages 11-12 and): all three are there. p.55 §4.2 Vowels: "Vowels tend to be longer in stressed final position than elsewhere in words of the same number of syllables." p.56 /ɛ/ allophone (ə): "Voiced mid close central un-rounded vocoid occurs in unstressed second syllable in multi-syllable words following non-dental laterals following /ɛ/ in initial syllable." (line-break hyphen in "un-rounded" only). Orthography chart last row: "/ˊ/ (stress).. is unmarked. is unmarked". The examples with final acute (pimí, wɛmbí, kuní, ɛpí, ouní, olsín..) and non-final ɛndéim are as reported. NEW: THE FULL PAPER IS NOW IN HAND. web.archive.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated in the accessible pages: the authors list stress (acute /ˊ/) among the phonemes, i.e. treat it as contrastive and mark it on every phonemic form, and refer to 'stressed final position' and to 'unstressed second syllable' in multi-syllable words. In the marked examples and the sample text the stress mark falls on the final syllable in the large majority of words (pimí, wɛmbí, kuní, ɛpí, ouní, olsín, rokú, nonomún, kongonúm, tonú, turúm, konú, tumbá, ením, maní, multún) but not always (ɛndéim 'one'; mbálus and mbalús 'airplane' both on p.77). The dedicated stress section (somewhere in pp. 60-76, not scanned) would settle whether stress is predictable (final) or lexical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in the accessible pages; only one acute per word is marked in the examples seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the accessible pages; the sample text (p.77) shows the same word 'airplane' as mbálus and mbalús.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: phonemic transcriptions of citation forms (pp. 46-59) and a connected sample text (pp. 77-78); the orthography leaves stress unmarked.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description is of the Nii (Ek Nii) language of the Western Highlands as worked on by the SIL Stucky team (Glottolog niii1240, ISO nii); the accessible pages name no dialect or village. Glottolog reference 36533 mislabels the volume as 'Studies in languages of the Ok family'; the SIL catalog line printed on the scans gives the actual volume title 'Phonologies of three languages of Papua New Guinea' (WPNGL 2, 108 pp.).

When the final syllable is a future suffix the primary stress falls on it and the secondary stress falls on the negative affix; in all other' / p.71: 'cases the primary stress falls on the negative affix and the secondary stress falls on…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Nii has an empty rule; the existing statement (from this same paper, p. 55-56 vowel-allophone remarks) reads 'lexical (unpredictable)'. The deciding sentence at pp. 70-71 confirms 'unpredictable' as the author's own word and adds detail not yet recorded: verb-final stress, secondary stress on negated verbs, and the pitch+intensity phonetic correlate. So: refines (compatible, adds the morphological sub-rule and secondary stress). Dialect: Monga dialect, informant Kusa of Kiam village (pp. 37-38).
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word (1-5 syllables), realised as higher pitch plus intensity; its position is lexically unpredictable in general. Sub-regularity: in verbs of two or more syllables stress is final; with a negative affix, primary stress goes to a final future suffix if present (negative affix takes secondary), otherwise primary stress goes to the negative affix and the final syllable takes secondary. Examples p. 71: /nonáɬmīn/ 'we didn't eat', /punēnmbí/ 'I will not go'; disyllables show both initial and final stress (/tómbu/ 'sweet potato', /ndambí/ 'green's', /éndi/ 'one', /endé/ 'the same'). p. 69: each syllable nucleus is a unit of potential stress placement; complex nuclei (/ai/, /ei/, /oi/..) bear a single stress. p. 40: complex nuclei carry one contrastive (high or rising) pitch, so pitch is contrastive at the nucleus level alongside stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, but only described for negated verbs: a secondary stress (marked ¯) falls on the negative affix when the word ends in a future suffix, otherwise on the final syllable (pp. 70-71).
new_statements.exceptions: The general statement is 'unpredictable'; the verb-final rule and the negative-affix rule are the only predictable cases given. Stress is unmarked in the proposed orthography (p. 73).
new_statements.identity_note: Stucky & Stucky 1973 describe Ek Nii of the Wahgi Valley (Kudjip to the Tuman river), Monga dialect, informant Kusa (c. 25 years old) of Kiam village (pp. 37-38). The 1970 ms. presumably covers the same variety (same authors, same fieldwork base) but was not opened.

tone_statements.citation: Cahill, Michael. 2011. Tonal diversity in languages of Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-008 (September 2011). Dallas: SIL International. 23 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Some languages are reported to have contrastive stress, such as Korafe (Farr and Farr 1974), Faiwol (Mecklenburg 1974), and Samo (Daniel and Shaw 1977). Nii (Stucky and Stucky 1973) is reported to have contrastive stress except on verbs, where it is predictable. Some have what may be labeled a pitch-accent system, e.g., Tinputz (Hostetler and Hostetler 1975), with one stress manifested as High tone per word (though some words lack this).
